common_name: Wichita Lineman Spuria Iris (Eric Nies Medal Yellow and Red-Brown Iris)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in late summer to early fall so roots establish before winter; spuria iris resent spring disturbance far more than bearded types.

directions: Hybridized by Jim Hedgecock from 'Falcon's Crest' crossed with 'Pieces of Eight' and registered in 2014, Wichita Lineman carries yellow, ruffled standards boldly streaked with red-brown radiating lines above medium purple style arms and gold falls heavily lined in red-brown with a narrow matching rim. The lightly sweet-scented flowers open in midseason on tall, sturdy stalks. It climbed through an Honorable Mention and an Award of Merit before taking the American Iris Society's Eric Nies Medal in 2025. Set rhizomes in deep, fertile soil kept moist through spring growth, and divide established clumps only occasionally, in late summer or early fall.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Red Warlord Spuria Iris (Eric Nies Medal Gold and Dark Red Iris)

planting.note: Plant or divide in late summer to early fall; spuria rhizomes establish poorly if disturbed during spring growth.

directions: Lee Walker bred Red Warlord from 'Highline Topaz' crossed with 'Duerme' and registered it in 2016, producing gold standards threaded with dark red veining and edged dark red-brown, style arms marked with a dark red center line and tip over cream-gold edges, and gold falls veined dark red clear to the rim. Blooming in midseason on stalks around 40 inches tall, it earned an Honorable Mention in 2019, an Award of Merit in 2021, and the American Iris Society's Eric Nies Medal in 2024. Give it deep, well-drained soil in full sun, and expect it to tolerate drier summer conditions better than most beardless iris once established.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Hot Chili Spuria Iris (Eric Nies Medal Red with Gold Signal Iris)

planting.note: Plant or divide in late summer to early fall for best establishment; avoid spring transplanting.

directions: Registered in 2014 by J. Terry Aitken from 'Innovator' crossed with 'Countess Zeppelin', Hot Chili bears chili-pepper red standards and style arms over falls in the same fiery red tone, set off by a yellow zonal patch and a gold dart-shaped signal. Reaching roughly 52 inches, it is one of the taller spuria cultivars and opens its flowers in late midseason. After an Honorable Mention in 2017 and an Award of Merit in 2019, it won the American Iris Society's Eric Nies Medal in 2023. Plant in full sun in deep, fertile ground; staking is rarely needed despite the height since the stalks are notably sturdy.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Ode To A Toad Spuria Iris (Eric Nies Medal Maroon and Orange-Gold Iris)

planting.note: Plant or divide in late summer to early fall so new roots are established before the ground freezes.

directions: Brad Kasperek registered Ode To A Toad in 2012 from a cross of 'Wyoming Cowboys' and 'Missouri Orange', giving it rich red-brown maroon standards, style arms mottled in brown and purple, and orange-gold falls rimmed and veined in smoky red-brown maroon, an unusual warm color break for the class. At a relatively compact 38 inches, it is shorter than many spuria cultivars and blooms in midseason. It earned an Honorable Mention in 2015, an Award of Merit in 2018, and the American Iris Society's Eric Nies Medal in 2022. Grow in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing clumps only when flowering starts to decline, typically after four or more years.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Mahogany Ember Spuria Iris (Eric Nies Medal Mahogany and Gold Iris)

planting.note: Plant or divide in late summer to early fall; this compact cultivar settles in fastest when given several weeks before frost.

directions: Lawrence Johnsen registered Mahogany Ember in 2011 from 'Tiffany May' crossed with 'Midnight Rival', introducing it commercially in 2013. Its standards are deep mahogany shading toward violet at the base, the style arms are yellow-tan with purple midribs, and the yellow-ground falls carry dense mahogany veining around a small golden-yellow signal flecked light brown, giving a compact, ruffled flower with real depth of color. Blooming in late midseason on stems under 40 inches, it moved through an Honorable Mention in 2018 and an Award of Merit in 2023 to win the American Iris Society's Eric Nies Medal in 2026. Site it in full sun in deep, moisture-retentive soil, and leave clumps undisturbed for several years before dividing.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Red War Clouds Spuria Iris (Eric Nies Medal Dark Red-Maroon Iris)

planting.note: Plant or divide in late summer to early fall for the strongest root establishment.

directions: Lee Walker registered Red War Clouds in 2009 from 'Zulu Chief' crossed with a seedling tracing back to 'Countess Zeppelin' and 'Pink Candles'. The lightly fragrant flowers combine dark red-maroon standards and falls with red-grey style arms tipped in red, centered on a medium yellow signal, opening in midseason on 40-inch stalks. It collected an Honorable Mention in 2013, an Award of Merit and the Niswonger Trophy in 2017, and the American Iris Society's Eric Nies Medal in 2019. Grow in full sun in deep, fertile soil, and divide congested clumps in late summer once bloom quality starts to taper off.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Lemon Chiffon Pie Spuria Iris (Eric Nies Medal Creamy Yellow Self Iris)

planting.note: Plant or divide bare-root rhizomes in late summer to early fall; spuria iris establish poorly from spring planting.

directions: Anna and David Cadd registered Lemon Chiffon Pie in 2006 from 'Media Luz' crossed with 'Candle Lace', producing a soft creamy yellow self with a large gold signal that blends gently into the cream ground, carried on ruffled petals. It blooms in midseason on stalks around 41 inches and rose through an Honorable Mention in 2010 and an Award of Merit in 2014 to win the American Iris Society's Eric Nies Medal in 2018. Plant in deep, fertile soil in full sun, where its pale color shows well against darker-flowered neighbors, and divide clumps only every four to five years.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: French Buttercream Pseudata Iris (Randolph-Perry Medal Pale Yellow Species-Cross Iris)

planting.note: Plant divisions in late summer to early fall into consistently moist, humus-rich soil; this sterile cultivar is propagated only by division, never by seed.

directions: Chad Harris registered French Buttercream in 2015 and introduced it in 2016 through Mt. Pleasant Iris Farm, a Pseudata cross sharing parentage with his own 'Violet Swallows'. A sterile, vigorous plant, it sends up fountains of foliage topped by two to three branched stems carrying nine to twelve buds of soft pale yellow, 4-to-5-inch flowers, each signal a bright yellow patch edged with faint violet eyelash markings, opening very late in the iris season on stalks up to five feet tall. After an Honorable Mention in 2021 and an Award of Merit in 2023, it won the American Iris Society's Randolph-Perry Medal in 2026. Grow it like a Japanese iris, in rich, consistently wet, slightly acidic soil at a pond margin or bog bed, since being sterile it relies entirely on division to propagate.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)
